blocks.content: The Composite Design Pattern is a structural pattern that lets you treat individual objects and groups of objects in exactly the same way.
It gives you the ability to build tree-shaped structures such as file systems, UI layouts, or org charts where a single element and a container full of elements both respond to the same operations.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245785531-c2642dc9.png
It becomes the right tool when:

["You are modeling structures where something can be either a single item or a collection of items.","You want to run the same operation across an entire hierarchy without caring whether a node is a leaf or a branch.","You want to get rid of messy conditional logic that checks \"is this a single object or a group\" before doing anything."]
items: You are modeling structures where something can be either a single item or a collection of items.
You want to run the same operation across an entire hierarchy without caring whether a node is a leaf or a branch.
You want to get rid of messy conditional logic that checks "is this a single object or a group" before doing anything.

blocks.content: Let's walk through a hands-on example and see how the Composite Pattern helps you build hierarchical systems that are clean, consistent, and easy to extend.
1. The Problem: Modeling an Organization Chart

The first instinct is to create two completely separate classes with no shared interface, and just type-check every item before operating on it:

blocks.content: Where This Design Falls Apart

1. Repetitive Type Checks Every single operation getSalary(), printStructure(), remove() is full of instanceof checks and casting. The same ugly pattern is copied across every method that walks the tree.
2. No Shared Abstraction Employee and Manager share no common interface. You cannot write clean generic code like:
3. Violates Open/Closed Principle Want to add a Contractor or Intern type? You must crack open the Manager class and add a new instanceof branch to every single method.

4. Fragile Recursive Logic Calculating total salary or removing a deeply nested team becomes a tangled web of nested conditionals. One missed type check and someone silently disappears from the payroll.
What We Actually Need
A cleaner design should:

["Introduce a shared interface like OrgMember that both Employee and Manager implement.","Let managers hold a list of OrgMember instead of raw Object references.","Support recursive operations with zero type checking.","Make adding new member types painless without touching any existing class."]
items: Let managers hold a list of OrgMember instead of raw Object references.
Support recursive operations with zero type checking.
Make adding new member types painless without touching any existing class.

blocks.content: This is exactly the problem the Composite Design Pattern was built to solve.
2. What is the Composite Pattern?
The Composite Pattern is a structural pattern that arranges objects into tree structures and lets clients interact with both individual items and entire groups through exactly the same interface.
Two core ideas define it:

1. Uniform Interface Both leaf nodes (no children) and composite nodes (contain children) implement the same interface. The client calls the same methods on a single employee or an entire department no special casing, no type checking.

2. Recursive Composition A composite holds a list of components, and each of those components can itself be a composite. This lets you build hierarchies of any depth without any extra handling at any level.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245785708-670484c8.png
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

blocks.content: The Four Participants

1. Component Interface OrgMember The shared contract that every node in the hierarchy must fulfill. It declares getSalary(), printStructure(), and remove(). The client only ever talks to this interface and never needs to know what sits behind it.

2. Leaf Employee The end node in the tree. It has no one reporting to it. It implements OrgMember directly returns its own salary, prints its own name, and removes itself. No delegation, no children, no complexity.

3. Composite Manager A node that holds a list of OrgMember objects and implements the same interface by passing work down to them. getSalary() adds up every report's salary. printStructure() prints the manager then asks each report to do the same. remove() clears the entire team then removes itself.

4. Client OrgChartApp Navigates and operates on the entire hierarchy through the OrgMember interface alone. It calls getSalary() on the CEO and gets the total company payroll. It has no idea whether it is dealing with a single employee or a department of fifty people.
3. How It Works
Here is the Composite workflow step by step, using our org chart example. The client calls one operation on the CEO and it ripples down through every manager and employee automatically.
Step 1: Build the tree The client creates leaf objects (Employee) and composite objects (Manager), then adds employees under their respective managers and managers under the CEO.
Step 2: Call an operation on the root The client calls getSalary() on the CEO. It does not need to know anything about the structure beneath.
Step 3: The composite delegates downward The CEO iterates over its direct reports Engineering Manager and Sales Manager and calls getSalary() on each one.
Step 4: Leaves return their values directly When getSalary() reaches Developer 1 or Sales Rep 2, the employee simply returns their own salary. No delegation, no further recursion.
Step 5: Nested composites keep recursing When getSalary() reaches a Manager, that manager calls getSalary() on each of their own reports and waits for every result to come back.

Step 6: Results bubble back up Each manager sums the salaries of their team and returns the total upward. Engineering Manager returns 155k, Sales Manager returns 115k, and the CEO gets the full company payroll of 270k from a single method call.
4. Implementing the Composite Pattern
Let's build the org chart system step by step, starting with a shared interface so every member of the hierarchy can be treated the same way.
Step 1: Define the Component Interface
Every node in the tree whether a single employee or an entire department implements this contract. No type checks, no special cases.
Step 2: Create the Leaf Class Employee
An employee is a leaf node. They have no reports, no delegation. They simply return their own data.
Step 3: Create the Composite Class Manager
A manager holds a list of OrgMember reports and implements every operation by delegating down to them. No instanceof, no casting just pure polymorphism.

Notice the difference from the naive approach. There is not a singleinstanceofcheck anywhere. TheManagersimply callsgetSalary()on each report. Polymorphism takes care of the rest whether the report is anEmployeeor anotherManager, the right implementation runs automatically.

blocks.content: What We Achieved

["Unified treatment Employees and managers share one interface, polymorphism does all the work","Clean recursion Zero instanceof checks, zero casting anywhere in the tree","Scalability Adding deeper nesting like a VP layer requires zero changes to existing code","Maintainability New member types like Contractor or Intern plug in without touching anything","Extensibility New operations can be added through interface extension without breaking the tree"]
items: Unified treatment Employees and managers share one interface, polymorphism does all the work
Clean recursion Zero instanceof checks, zero casting anywhere in the tree
Scalability Adding deeper nesting like a VP layer requires zero changes to existing code
Maintainability New member types like Contractor or Intern plug in without touching anything
Extensibility New operations can be added through interface extension without breaking the tree

blocks.content: 5. Practical Example: University Hierarchy

To see the Composite pattern in a completely different setting, let's model a university structure. A UniversityComponentinterface is shared by Professor (leaf) and Department (composite). Departments can contain professors and other departments, forming a tree that represents the entire university.

The system supports three operations: getBudget() computes the total budget for a node and everything beneath it, getHeadcount() counts all people in that branch, and printHierarchy() displays the structure with indentation.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245785986-26e6cc80.png

      - Bob (Lecturer, $75000)
    - Charlie (Researcher, $70000)
  + Science Faculty (Dean, $150000)
    - Diana (Lab Director, $95000)

blocks.content: Notice how the samegetBudget()call works at any level. Calling it on the Rector gives the entire university's spend. Calling it on a single faculty gives just that department's cost. The client code stays identical at every level. That is exactly what makes Composite so powerful the same operation scales effortlessly from a single professor all the way up to the entire institution.
